passages.happening:
“Then Joseph could no longer control himself before all his attendants, and he cried out, ‘Send everyone away from me!’” (verse 1). He is alone with his brothers when he makes himself known.

“But he wept so loudly that the Egyptians heard him, and Pharaoh's household soon heard of it” (verse 2).

“Joseph said to his brothers, ‘I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?’ But they were unable to answer him, because they were terrified in his presence” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Judah's speech has broken Joseph's control. He has watched a brother offer his own freedom for Benjamin. The test is over.

He sends the Egyptians out. What happens next is family business. It is also his brothers' shame, and he does not make it public.

But he cannot keep it quiet. He weeps so loudly that the whole house hears. A great official of Egypt was expected to keep his feelings to himself. Joseph cannot.

Then three words in Hebrew: ‘I am Joseph.’ No title. No Egyptian name. Just the name his mother gave him.

His first question is about his father. Judah has just spoken of the old man as if his life hung by a thread. Joseph needs to hear it again: is he still alive?

The brothers cannot speak. ‘Terrified’ is the right word. The boy they sold now holds their lives in his hand, and he knows everything they did.
passages.later:
Stephen tells this moment in Acts: “On their second visit, Joseph revealed his identity to his brothers, and his family became known to Pharaoh” (Acts 7:13).

When the risen Jesus stood among his frightened followers, the ones who had run away, he said, “Look at My hands and My feet. It is I Myself” (Luke 24:39).
passages.asks: Joseph made himself known in private, and spared his brothers a public shame. Ask whether, when you confront someone who wronged you, you seek to expose them or to restore them. Then ask what it would take to choose the second.

passages.t: ‘It was not you who sent me here, but God’
passages.happening:
“Then Joseph said to his brothers, ‘Please come near me.’ And they did so. ‘I am Joseph, your brother,’ he said, ‘the one you sold into Egypt!’” (verse 4).

“And now, do not be distressed or angry with yourselves that you sold me into this place, because it was to save lives that God sent me before you” (verse 5).

The famine has lasted two years, and five more are coming (verse 6). “God sent me before you to preserve you as a remnant on the earth and to save your lives by a great deliverance” (verse 7).

“Therefore it was not you who sent me here, but God” (verse 8). God has made him “a father to Pharaoh” and ruler over all Egypt (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
‘Please come near me.’ The brothers have backed away in fear. Joseph calls them close.

Then he says the hard thing first. ‘The one you sold into Egypt.’ He does not pretend it did not happen. He names their act plainly, before he says anything about God.

Only then does he tell them what God was doing. Three times he says that God sent him (verses 5, 7, 8). The brothers ‘sold’. God ‘sent’. One event, two actors, two purposes.

A remnant is what is left over: the few who survive so that a people can go on. Without Joseph's grain, Jacob's family would have died, and with them the promise God made to Abraham.

‘A father to Pharaoh’ means a trusted adviser, someone whose counsel the king relies on. The Bible uses ‘father’ in this way for a high official elsewhere too (Isaiah 22:21).

And notice what Joseph does not say. He does not say, ‘It was nothing.’ He does not say they did no wrong. He says, ‘Do not be distressed or angry with yourselves.’ He speaks to men who are terrified of his revenge. He is not excusing their sin. He is refusing to let their guilt be the last word.
passages.later:
Peter spoke in the same way about the cross: Jesus “was delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge, and you, by the hands of the lawless, put Him to death by nailing Him to the cross” (Acts 2:23). God's purpose and human guilt stand together in both stories, and neither cancels the other.

A psalm sees the same hand: “He sent a man before them” (Psalm 105:17).
passages.hard:
If God sent Joseph, are the brothers excused? No. Two things stand side by side here, as they did in chapter 27, and the text does not let either one cancel the other. The brothers sold their brother, and that was evil. God used it to save many lives, and that was good. Joseph names the sale before he names God.

Christians explain how these fit in more than one way. The Reformed tradition says that God ordains all that comes to pass, even evil acts, without being the author of sin and without taking away human guilt. Arminian, and many Catholic and Orthodox, theologians prefer to say that God permits evil acts he does not will, and then overrules them for good. These notes take no side. On both accounts the brothers did wrong, and God's purpose was not defeated by it. The note on Genesis 50:15-21 says more.

Forgiveness here is real. But forgiving is not the same as saying the wrong did not matter. Joseph forgives men he has watched change. He saw Judah offer himself in Benjamin's place.

A word of care. Forgiving someone does not mean going back to a person who is still dangerous. Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice.

If you are being hurt in some other place, at home, at work or in a church, the same is true. Tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Joseph named the wrong plainly and then refused to let it have the last word. Ask whether there is a wrong done to you that you have either pretended did not matter, or let define everything since. Then ask what it would mean to do what Joseph did, and to do it safely.

passages.happening:
Joseph sends a message to his father: “This is what your son Joseph says: God has made me lord of all Egypt. Come down to me without delay” (verse 9).

“You shall settle in the land of Goshen and be near me” (verse 10). There are five more years of famine, and Joseph will provide for them (verse 11).

He tells his brothers to report all his splendor in Egypt, “And bring my father down here quickly” (verse 13).

“Then Joseph threw his arms around his brother Benjamin and wept, and Benjamin wept as they embraced” (verse 14). “Joseph kissed each of his brothers as he wept over them. And afterward his brothers talked with him” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Goshen was a region of Egypt. It is usually placed in the eastern Nile delta, the wide, green land where the river splits into branches before reaching the sea. Its exact borders are not known. It was good grazing land, on the side of Egypt nearest to Canaan.

Notice how often Joseph says ‘my father’ and ‘quickly’. Twenty years of separation are pressing on him.

Then the embrace. He weeps on Benjamin first, his mother's son. Then he kisses every one of the brothers who sold him, and weeps over each one.

And then the last line: ‘afterward his brothers talked with him.’ Look back to chapter 37. The brothers ‘could not speak a kind word to him’ (37:4). After twenty years of silence and lies, they are talking.
passages.later:
Jesus told of a father who saw his lost son coming home, “ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him” (Luke 15:20).

Paul writes, “Be kind and tenderhearted to one another, forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32).
passages.asks: The story that began with brothers who could not speak kindly ends with brothers who talk. Ask whether there is a silence in your family that has lasted for years. Then ask what one honest, kind conversation might begin.

passages.happening:
News reaches Pharaoh's house that Joseph's brothers have come. “Pharaoh and his servants were pleased” (verse 16).

Pharaoh tells Joseph to send for the whole family: “I will give you the best of the land of Egypt, and you shall eat from the fat of the land” (verse 18). They are to take wagons from Egypt for the children and wives (verse 19). “But pay no regard to your belongings, for the best of all the land of Egypt is yours” (verse 20).

Joseph gives each brother new clothes, “but to Benjamin he gave three hundred shekels of silver and five sets of clothes” (verse 22). He sends loaded donkeys to his father (verse 23).

As they leave, he says, “Do not quarrel on the way!” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Pharaoh is glad. Joseph saved his country, and Pharaoh honors his family. ‘The fat of the land’ means its richest food.

Wagons were carts with wheels, pulled by animals. Seeing Egyptian wagons will be the proof that convinces Jacob.

Notice the clothes again. Joseph's story could be told through clothing. His brothers stripped off his robe and dipped it in blood. Now he clothes every one of them.

And Benjamin gets more again: silver and five sets of clothes. Once, a special gift of clothing to Rachel's son made the brothers hate him. This time no one complains.

Then a short word as they go. ‘Do not quarrel on the way.’ The Hebrew word can mean to be stirred up, whether by anger or by fear. Some take it as a warning not to blame one another for the past. Others take it as ‘Do not be afraid on the road’. Both suit men who must now go home and tell their father the truth.
passages.later: Paul writes, “Bear with one another and forgive any complaint you may have against someone else. Forgive as the Lord forgave you” (Colossians 3:13). And, “If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone” (Romans 12:18).
passages.asks: Joseph knew his brothers might start blaming one another on the road home. Ask where, after a wrong has been forgiven, you keep reopening it with others. Then ask what it would mean to let it stay closed.

passages.happening:
The brothers come home to Jacob. “Joseph is still alive,” they say, “and he is ruler over all the land of Egypt!” (verse 26). “But Jacob was stunned, for he did not believe them” (verse 26).

They tell him all that Joseph said, “and when he saw the wagons that Joseph had sent to carry him back, the spirit of their father Jacob was revived” (verse 27).

“‘Enough!’ declared Israel. ‘My son Joseph is still alive! I will go to see him before I die’” (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Did the brothers also tell their father how Joseph came to Egypt? The text does not say. Genesis never shows that conversation. It only shows Jacob's shock.

‘Stunned’ is a strong word. In Hebrew it says his heart grew numb, or cold. He had believed his sons once, about the robe. Now, when they tell the truth, he cannot believe them.

The wagons change his mind. Words were not enough. He needed to see something.

Then ‘the spirit of their father Jacob was revived.’ For twenty years he had said he would go down to the grave mourning. Now life comes back into him.

And notice the name. The narrator calls him ‘Jacob’ when he is stunned, and ‘Israel’ when he decides. Israel is the name God gave him, the name of the one who carries the promise (32:28).
passages.later: On the first Easter, the women told the apostles that Jesus was alive, “But their words seemed like nonsense to them, and they did not believe the women” (Luke 24:11). Good news can be too good to believe at first.
passages.asks: Jacob could not believe the good news until he saw the wagons. Ask whether there is good news about God that you find too good to believe. Then ask what signs of it you have already been given.
